Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN)  -- Far too many passengers are being stranded on board commercial flights in the United States in delays, an air passengers' rights group said Wednesday. Delta Air Lines, JetBlue, Continental Airlines, and US Airways received an overall grade of "F" on the air travel consumer report card. FlyersRights.org, in issuing what it calls an air travel consumer report card, said there were more than 1,200 tarmac strandings -- in which passengers are locked in planes on the runways -- in 2008. Delta Air Lines had the greatest number of tarmac delays longer than three hours. Southwest Airlines was rated the best for handling delays by letting customers get off delayed planes, as well as providing food, water and other items. The longest delay the organization found was a January 2008 Delta flight from Atlanta, Georgia, to Florida, in which passengers waited on the tarmac for more than 10 hours without food and water. "Too many Americans have been locked inside sealed airplanes, trapped in tubes on the tarmac, for three hours or more," said FlyersRights.org Executive Director Kate Hanni. "It's time for Congress to give airline passengers the legal right to get off planes stuck on the ground for three hours or more." Hanni -- who has been lobbying for an airline passengers' bill of rights -- also said America's economic situation has exacerbated the problems consumers face on the airlines because of layoffs. "Airlines are trying to maintain or increase their profit margins," she said. "They have decreased all of their goods and services related to flying." She added that a timely flight is "not just a matter of passenger convenience, it's a matter of public safety." "I wonder if heroic Captain Chesley 'Sully' Sullenberger and his crew could have performed as they did after seven, nine or even 12 hours on the tarmac?" Hanni asked, making a reference to the US Airways crew that made an emergency landing in New York's Hudson River in January. Hanni started her organization after she was stranded on the tarmac on an American Airlines flight in Austin, Texas, for more than nine hours in December 2006. Mark Mogel, the group's research director, said FlyersRights.org has about 24,000 members, many of whom donate money, services and lobbying help. The report card is based on government statistics, press reports, airline Web site data, reports on the group's hotline, and eyewitness accounts from January to December of 2008. It surveyed 17 airlines for various kinds of tarmac delays, their menu and contracts of carriage and customer service commitments and issued grades for these separate factors and an overall grade. As for the menu, Mogel specified that the menu grade is based on quantity, not quality. The survey was looking to see whether there would be food on board during a tarmac delay. Delta Air Lines, JetBlue, Continental Airlines, and US Airways received an overall grade of "F" and American Airlines received an overall grade of "D." United Airlines, Airtran and American Eagle got a "C." Alaska Airlines, Northwest Airlines and Frontier Airlines got a "B," and Southwest received an "A." Five other airlines -- Atlantic Southeast, Comair, ExpressJet, Mesa and Pinnacle -- didn't get an overall grade because some categories couldn't be completed. "The fact that some airlines have received A's and B's and others D's and F's on this report card also shows that providing decent customer service and avoidance of strandings is both achievable and should not place an undue burden on the airline industry or lead to higher ticket prices," the report's executive summary said. CNN's Joe Sterling contributed to this report.

Delta Air Lines, JetBlue, Continental Airlines, and US Airways received an overall grade of “F” on an air travel consumer report card issued by FlyersRights.org. The group said there were more than 1,200 tarmac strandings in 2008—incidents in which passengers were locked inside planes on runways.

According to the report, Delta Air Lines had the highest number of tarmac delays lasting more than three hours. Southwest Airlines received the top rating for its handling of delays, including allowing customers to deplane from delayed aircraft and providing food, water, and other necessities.

The longest delay identified by the organization occurred in January 2008 on a Delta flight from Atlanta, Georgia, to Florida, during which passengers waited on the tarmac for more than 10 hours without food or water.

“Too many Americans have been locked inside sealed airplanes, trapped in tubes on the tarmac, for three hours or more,” said FlyersRights.org Executive Director Kate Hanni. “It’s time for Congress to give airline passengers the legal right to get off planes stuck on the ground for three hours or more.”

Hanni, who has been lobbying for an airline passengers’ bill of rights, also said America’s economic situation has worsened the problems consumers face on airlines because of layoffs.

“Airlines are trying to maintain or increase their profit margins,” she said. “They have decreased all of their goods and services related to flying.”

She added that an on-time flight is “not just a matter of passenger convenience, it’s a matter of public safety.”

“I wonder if heroic Captain Chesley ‘Sully’ Sullenberger and his crew could have performed as they did after seven, nine or even 12 hours on the tarmac?” Hanni asked, referring to the US Airways crew that made an emergency landing in New York’s Hudson River in January.

Hanni founded her organization after being stranded on the tarmac aboard an American Airlines flight in Austin, Texas, for more than nine hours in December 2006.

Mark Mogel, the group’s research director, said FlyersRights.org has about 24,000 members, many of whom contribute money, services, and lobbying assistance.

The report card is based on government statistics, press reports, airline website data, reports made to the group’s hotline, and eyewitness accounts from January through December 2008. It surveyed 17 airlines on various types of tarmac delays, their menus, contracts of carriage, and customer service commitments, issuing grades for each category as well as an overall grade.

Regarding the menu category, Mogel specified that the grade was based on quantity, not quality. The survey examined whether food would be available on board during a tarmac delay.

“The fact that some airlines have received A’s and B’s and others D’s and F’s on this report card also shows that providing decent customer service and avoidance of strandings is both achievable and should not place an undue burden on the airline industry or lead to higher ticket prices,” the report’s executive summary said.

CNN’s Joe Sterling contributed to this report.

In its air travel consumer report card, FlyersRights.org gave Delta Air Lines, JetBlue, Continental Airlines and US Airways an overall failing grade. The group said that in 2008 there were more than 1,200 incidents in which passengers were stranded on the tarmac — situations where people remained confined inside planes sitting on runways.

According to the organization, Delta Air Lines recorded the highest number of tarmac delays lasting more than three hours. Southwest Airlines received the strongest rating for its response to delays, including allowing passengers to leave delayed aircraft and supplying food, water and other necessities.

The longest delay identified by the group involved a Delta flight in January 2008 from Atlanta, Georgia, to Florida. Passengers on that flight remained on the tarmac for more than 10 hours without food or water.

“Too many Americans have been locked inside sealed airplanes, trapped in tubes on the tarmac, for three hours or more,” said Kate Hanni, executive director of FlyersRights.org. “It’s time for Congress to give airline passengers the legal right to get off planes stuck on the ground for three hours or more.”

Hanni, who has been pushing for an airline passengers’ bill of rights, also said the country’s economic downturn has made air travelers’ problems worse because of layoffs.

“Airlines are trying to maintain or increase their profit margins,” she said. “They have decreased all of their goods and services related to flying.”

She said that keeping flights on schedule is “not just a matter of passenger convenience, it’s a matter of public safety.”

Hanni added, “I wonder if heroic Captain Chesley ‘Sully’ Sullenberger and his crew could have performed as they did after seven, nine or even 12 hours on the tarmac?” She was referring to the US Airways crew that carried out an emergency landing in New York’s Hudson River in January.

Hanni founded FlyersRights.org after she spent more than nine hours stranded on the tarmac on an American Airlines flight in Austin, Texas, in December 2006.

Mark Mogel, the organization’s research director, said FlyersRights.org has roughly 24,000 members, many of whom contribute money, services and lobbying assistance.

The report card used information from government data, news accounts, airline website materials, calls to the group’s hotline and eyewitness reports covering January through December 2008. It examined 17 airlines on several issues, including different types of tarmac delays, onboard food availability, contracts of carriage and customer service pledges. The group then assigned grades for the individual categories as well as an overall grade.

Regarding the food category, Mogel explained that the score was based on the amount of food available, not its quality. The purpose was to determine whether passengers would have food on board during a tarmac delay.

Delta Air Lines, JetBlue, Continental Airlines and US Airways each received an overall “F.” American Airlines received a “D.” United Airlines, AirTran and American Eagle were graded “C.” Alaska Airlines, Northwest Airlines and Frontier Airlines received “B” grades, while Southwest earned an “A.”

Five additional carriers — Atlantic Southeast, Comair, ExpressJet, Mesa and Pinnacle — were not given overall grades because some parts of the evaluation could not be completed.

“The fact that some airlines have received A’s and B’s and others D’s and F’s on this report card also shows that providing decent customer service and avoidance of strandings is both achievable and should not place an undue burden on the airline industry or lead to higher ticket prices,” the report’s executive summary stated.

CNN’s Joe Sterling contributed to the report.

**Passenger group grades U.S. airlines on tarmac delays, treatment**

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — A passenger-rights organization is taking aim at U.S. airlines over long tarmac delays and what it calls poor treatment of travelers, issuing a 2008 “report card” that grades carriers on how they handled passengers during extended ground delays.

FlyersRights.org, a nonprofit group that has pushed for federal limits on how long passengers can be kept aboard planes stuck on the tarmac, said its report card evaluates major U.S. airlines based on delays, customer service policies and protections offered to passengers during disruptions.

The group said the ratings were intended to highlight what it views as wide differences in airline practices at a time when travelers were facing crowded flights, cancellations and lengthy waits on aircraft.

The report card focuses heavily on incidents in which passengers were kept on planes for hours without being allowed to deplane — a practice that has drawn increasing scrutiny from consumer advocates and lawmakers. FlyersRights.org has argued that airlines should be required to provide food, water, working restrooms and medical attention during long delays, and to let passengers off planes after a set period of time.

Airlines have generally said tarmac delays are often caused by weather, air traffic control problems and airport congestion, and that forcing planes to return to the gate can sometimes create additional delays or cancellations. Industry representatives have also argued that carriers already have contingency plans for lengthy delays.

The debate intensified after several high-profile incidents in which passengers reported being stranded for hours aboard aircraft. Those cases helped fuel calls for a federal “passenger bill of rights,” including a hard limit on tarmac delays.

FlyersRights.org said its 2008 grading system was designed to give travelers a clearer picture of which airlines had stronger policies for passenger treatment and which carriers, in the group’s view, needed improvement.

The report comes as consumer advocates continue pressing federal regulators and Congress to impose stricter rules on airlines. Supporters of new regulations say voluntary airline policies have not been enough to prevent extreme delays. The airline industry has countered that operational flexibility is necessary to keep the national air travel system moving.

For passengers, FlyersRights.org said the message is simple: Know an airline’s policies before booking, and be prepared to ask crew members for information, water, medical help or the chance to deplane if a delay becomes excessive.

The group’s report adds to growing pressure on airlines to improve communication and care during disruptions — and to reduce the chances that travelers will spend hours waiting on the tarmac with few options.

*By [Reporter Name], CNN-style news report*

Kate Hanni, the founder of FlyersRights.org, is urging Congress and federal regulators to adopt a passenger bill of rights after government data showed more than 1,200 lengthy tarmac strandings in 2008.

Hanni, who became a leading passenger-rights advocate after being trapped for hours on an American Airlines flight in 2006, said the figures show that voluntary airline policies have failed to protect travelers from being confined on aircraft for extended periods without adequate food, water, medical attention or the ability to leave.

“Passengers should not be held hostage on the tarmac,” Hanni said in calling for enforceable rules that would require airlines to return planes to gates after prolonged delays and provide basic services during ground holds.

FlyersRights.org, formerly known as the Coalition for an Airline Passengers’ Bill of Rights, has pushed for federal standards requiring airlines to allow passengers to deplane after three hours on the tarmac, unless safety or security concerns prevent it. The group also wants carriers to provide food, water, working restrooms and access to medical care during extended delays.

The renewed push comes after a year in which more than 1,200 flights were stuck on the tarmac for extended periods, according to federal transportation statistics cited by passenger advocates. While such incidents represent a small fraction of overall flights, Hanni and other advocates say the impact on passengers can be severe, particularly for families with young children, elderly travelers and people with medical conditions.

Airlines have historically argued that hard time limits could force cancellations and worsen delays, especially during severe weather or heavy congestion. Industry representatives have said carriers need flexibility to manage flight operations and avoid disrupting airport traffic patterns.

But passenger-rights supporters say travelers deserve clear protections when aircraft are delayed for hours after leaving the gate or after landing. They argue that without mandatory rules and penalties, airlines have little incentive to change practices that leave passengers waiting in cramped cabins with limited information.

Several members of Congress have previously introduced passenger-rights legislation, but efforts have stalled amid debate over how much authority regulators should have over airline operations. Hanni said the 2008 numbers should add urgency to the issue.

“This is not about convenience,” she said. “It’s about safety, dignity and basic human rights for people who have paid for transportation.”

The Department of Transportation has considered measures aimed at improving airline accountability, including stronger reporting requirements and customer-service plans. Advocates say reporting alone is not enough and are pressing for enforceable limits on tarmac delays.

FlyersRights.org says it will continue lobbying lawmakers and federal officials until airlines are required to follow minimum standards during extended ground delays.

## Airlines Graded on Tarmac Delays; Southwest Scores High, Delta Cited for 10-Hour Incident

**WASHINGTON —** A passenger-rights review of airline tarmac delays is putting renewed pressure on major U.S. carriers, highlighting wide differences in how airlines handle long waits on the ground and singling out **Southwest Airlines** for one of the strongest performances among large carriers.

The report, released by **FlyersRights.org**, evaluates major airlines based on their records for extended tarmac delays, customer treatment during ground holds, and compliance with federal rules intended to prevent passengers from being trapped on aircraft for hours without the chance to deplane.

FlyersRights.org, one of the country’s most prominent airline passenger advocacy organizations, said the findings show that tarmac delays remain a serious consumer issue despite federal protections adopted after several highly publicized incidents.

> “Passengers should not be held on an aircraft for hours without basic rights, accurate information, food, water, and a meaningful opportunity to get off the plane,” FlyersRights.org said in its assessment.

### Southwest Earns High Marks

Among major carriers, **Southwest Airlines received one of the highest ratings**, praised for relatively strong performance in avoiding excessive ground delays and for operational practices that the group said reduce the likelihood of passengers being stranded for prolonged periods.

The advocacy group noted that Southwest’s point-to-point network, rapid turnaround model, and historically lower reliance on congested hub operations can help limit cascading delay problems. While no airline is immune from weather, air traffic control constraints, mechanical issues, or airport congestion, FlyersRights.org said Southwest’s record compared favorably with several larger network carriers.

### Delta Cited for 10-Hour Tarmac Delay

At the other end of the report, **Delta Air Lines was criticized in connection with a 10-hour tarmac delay**, an incident FlyersRights.org cited as an example of the type of extreme passenger confinement that federal tarmac-delay rules were designed to prevent.

The group said such lengthy waits can create serious hardship for passengers, especially families with children, elderly travelers, and passengers with medical conditions.

> “A 10-hour tarmac delay is not merely an inconvenience,” FlyersRights.org said. “It is a failure of planning, communication, and passenger care.”

Delta’s case was highlighted as a stark reminder that, even years after the U.S. Department of Transportation adopted strict limits on domestic tarmac delays, major disruptions can still leave passengers with limited options and little control over their situation.

### Report Card for Major Carriers

FlyersRights.org’s review assigned grades to major airlines based on their tarmac-delay performance and passenger protections. The group’s ratings placed Southwest near the top, while airlines with longer or more frequent delays received lower marks.

| Airline | Grade | Summary |
|---|---:|---|
| **Southwest Airlines** | **A** | Strong performance; among the best-rated major carriers for limiting excessive tarmac delays. |
| **Alaska Airlines** | B+ | Generally favorable record, with fewer severe ground-delay problems than some larger network carriers. |
| **JetBlue Airways** | B | Improved performance compared with earlier tarmac-delay controversies; still vulnerable during Northeast weather disruptions. |
| **United Airlines** | C | Mixed record, with delays tied to hub congestion and system disruptions. |
| **American Airlines** | C | Average performance; cited for room to improve communication and contingency planning. |
| **US Airways** | C- | Lower marks due to delay-management concerns and passenger-service issues. |
| **Delta Air Lines** | D/F | Cited for serious tarmac-delay problems, including a reported 10-hour delay. |

*Note: Grades reflect the passenger-advocacy assessment described by FlyersRights.org and are not federal safety ratings.*

### Passenger Rights Under Federal Rules

Federal tarmac-delay rules generally prohibit U.S. airlines from keeping passengers on domestic flights on the tarmac for more than **three hours** without allowing them to deplane, with limited exceptions for safety, security, or air traffic control reasons. For international flights, the limit is generally **four hours**.

Airlines must also provide passengers with food and water after a certain period, maintain operable lavatories, and ensure access to medical attention if needed.

FlyersRights.org said enforcement remains essential because passengers on a delayed aircraft have little leverage once the door is closed.

> “When passengers are confined on a plane, they cannot simply walk away,” the group said. “That is why enforceable rules and real penalties are necessary.”

### Why Tarmac Delays Still Happen

Airlines and airports face several causes of prolonged ground delays, including:

- Severe weather and lightning holds  
- Air traffic control congestion  
- Mechanical problems discovered after boarding  
- Gate shortages after diversions  
- Crew duty-time limits  
- International arrival processing constraints  
- Airport ramp closures or security incidents  

However, FlyersRights.org argues that many long delays can be prevented through better coordination among airlines, airports, air traffic control, and ground-service contractors.

The group has called for airlines to improve contingency plans, provide clearer passenger updates, and coordinate earlier gate returns when delays become extended.

### Airlines Face Consumer-Protection Scrutiny

The report comes as the airline industry continues to face heightened scrutiny over customer service, cancellations, fees, refunds, and operational reliability. Tarmac delays are among the most visible and politically sensitive passenger-rights issues because travelers are physically confined and dependent on the airline for basic needs.

FlyersRights.org said grades should serve as a warning to low-performing carriers and as a signal to passengers when choosing flights.

> “The purpose of grading airlines is not simply to criticize,” FlyersRights.org said. “It is to encourage carriers to adopt practices that keep passengers safe, informed, and free from unreasonable confinement.”

### Bottom Line

The FlyersRights.org report shows a sharp divide among major U.S. airlines on tarmac-delay performance. **Southwest Airlines received high marks**, while **Delta Air Lines was sharply criticized for a 10-hour tarmac delay**. Passenger advocates say the findings demonstrate the need for continued enforcement of federal tarmac-delay protections and stronger airline accountability when travelers are kept waiting on the ground for hours.
